gloss: The meat of a cow, bull, or steer.
examples: We grill *beef* about once a week in the summer.
This stew tastes better with *beef* than with chicken.
The price of *beef* has gone up again.

gloss: The meat of a pig.
examples: She marinated the *pork* overnight in soy sauce and garlic.
*Pork* is cheaper than beef at our store.
He doesn't eat *pork* for religious reasons.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A young sheep, or the meat that comes from one.
examples: We had roast *lamb* with mint sauce for Easter.
The *lambs* were out in the field by March.
*Lamb* has a stronger flavor than beef.
contrast: The b is silent — LAM, exactly like the first half of "lamp" without the p.

gloss: The pale meat of a young calf.
examples: The restaurant is famous for its breaded *veal*.
*Veal* is more delicate than beef.
A lot of people won't order *veal* on principle.

gloss: The meat of a fully grown sheep.
examples: *Mutton* is much harder to find in American stores than lamb.
The curry was made with *mutton* and potatoes.
My grandfather grew up eating *mutton* every Sunday.

gloss: The meat of a deer.
examples: My uncle gave us a freezer full of *venison* after hunting season.
*Venison* is leaner than beef, so don't overcook it.
She made chili with ground *venison*.

gloss: Chicken, turkey, duck and other farm birds raised for meat or eggs.
examples: Wash your hands after handling raw *poultry*.
The *poultry* section is at the back of the store.
Prices for *poultry* stayed flat all year.

gloss: A thick flat cut of meat, usually beef, meant for grilling or frying.
examples: He ordered a *steak* medium rare.
The *steaks* need about four minutes a side.
I could eat *steak* every night of the week.
contrast: Sounds exactly like "stake" (кол, ставка) — STAYK, not "steek".

gloss: Salted or smoked meat from the back or sides of a pig, usually sliced thin.
examples: The whole house smelled like *bacon*.
Do you want *bacon* on your burger?
She fried six strips of *bacon* for breakfast.

gloss: Salted or smoked meat from the upper leg of a pig.
examples: I'll take a *ham* and cheese sandwich.
We baked a whole *ham* for the holidays.
There's some sliced *ham* in the fridge.

gloss: Ground meat mixed with spices and packed into a thin skin.
examples: Breakfast was eggs, toast, and *sausage*.
The *sausages* burst open on the grill.
He puts spicy Italian *sausage* in his pasta sauce.

gloss: A cooked patty of ground beef served in a round bun.
examples: I'll have a *hamburger* and fries.
The kids ate three *hamburgers* between them.
You can get a decent *hamburger* at that diner for six bucks.

gloss: A hamburger, or any sandwich built on a similar patty.
examples: Let's grab a *burger* after the game.
Their veggie *burgers* are surprisingly good.
He flipped the *burger* too early and it fell apart.

gloss: A hamburger with a slice of melted cheese on the patty.
examples: One *cheeseburger*, no onions, please.
The *cheeseburgers* here come with bacon by default.
He ate half a *cheeseburger* and gave up.

gloss: A cooked sausage served in a long soft bun.
examples: We got *hot dogs* at the ballpark.
He put ketchup on his *hot dog* and everyone judged him.
There's a cart on the corner that sells *hot dogs* all night.

gloss: A small ball of ground meat, usually cooked in sauce or soup.
examples: She rolled the *meatballs* by hand.
I'll take a *meatball* sub with extra sauce.
The *meatballs* simmered in the pot all afternoon.

gloss: Ground meat mixed with bread and seasonings, then baked in a loaf shape.
examples: *Meatloaf* and mashed potatoes is classic diner food.
My mom's *meatloaf* recipe hasn't changed in forty years.
He made two *meatloaves* and froze one.
contrast: Plural follows loaf → loaves: *meatloaves*, not "meatloafs".

gloss: A small flat round piece of ground meat, shaped for frying or grilling.
examples: Press the *patty* down with a spatula.
These *patties* are a quarter pound each.
The burger came with two *patties* and no cheese.

gloss: Beef that has been chopped very fine in a grinder.
examples: Brown the *ground beef* before you add the onions.
I picked up a pound of *ground beef* for tacos.
This recipe works with *ground beef* or ground turkey.
contrast: American *ground beef* is British "minced beef" or just "mince".

gloss: Beef brisket cured in salt brine.
examples: *Corned beef* and cabbage is a St. Patrick's Day tradition here.
The deli slices their *corned beef* paper thin.
He made hash out of the leftover *corned beef*.

gloss: Beef cooked in an oven in one large piece, often served sliced.
examples: Sunday dinner was *roast beef* and gravy.
I'll take *roast beef* on rye with mustard.
There's cold *roast beef* left over from last night.

gloss: Sliced cooked or cured meats eaten cold, usually in sandwiches.
examples: Grab some *cold cuts* and a loaf of bread.
The tray was piled with *cold cuts* and cheese.
We lived on *cold cuts* the whole week we were moving.
contrast: Used in the plural — Americans say "some *cold cuts*", almost never "a cold cut".

gloss: A cut of beef from the lower chest, usually cooked slowly.
examples: The *brisket* smoked for twelve hours.
She braises a *brisket* every Passover.
Texas barbecue is really about the *brisket*.

gloss: A cut of beef from the back, between the ribs and the rump.
examples: *Sirloin* is a good compromise between price and tenderness.
He grilled two *sirloins* for dinner.
The special was a ten-ounce *sirloin* with a baked potato.

gloss: The long, very tender muscle running along the backbone.
examples: Pork *tenderloin* cooks in about twenty minutes.
She tied the *tenderloin* with string before roasting it.
*Tenderloin* is the most expensive cut on the menu.

gloss: A steak cut from the rib section, known for its marbling.
examples: He always orders the *ribeye*.
Two *ribeyes* cost more than the rest of the groceries.
A *ribeye* has enough fat that you barely need oil.

gloss: A curved bone from an animal's chest, with the meat attached, eaten as food.
examples: We ordered a full rack of *ribs*.
The *ribs* fell right off the bone.
He gnawed on one last *rib* and gave up.

gloss: A thick slice of meat, usually pork or lamb, cut with the bone still in.
examples: She pan-fried two pork *chops* in butter.
The lamb *chop* was cooked perfectly.
*Chops* dry out fast, so watch the heat.

gloss: A thin, boneless piece of meat, often breaded and fried.
examples: Pound the chicken *cutlets* until they're even.
The veal *cutlet* came with lemon on the side.
She breaded six *cutlets* and fried them in batches.

gloss: The cut of meat from an animal's back, on either side of the spine.
examples: Pork *loin* is on sale this week.
He roasted a whole *loin* with rosemary.
The butcher cut the *loin* into chops for me.

gloss: The lower part of an animal's leg, cooked slowly as a cut of meat.
examples: Lamb *shanks* need three hours in the oven.
He braised the *shank* in red wine.
A *shank* is cheap, but you can't rush it.

gloss: A lean cut of beef from the belly area below the ribs.
examples: *Flank* steak is best sliced against the grain.
She marinated the *flank* for two hours.
Grill the *flank* hot and fast.

gloss: A large piece of meat cooked whole in an oven.
examples: The *roast* has been in the oven since noon.
She bought a five-pound *roast* for Sunday.
Both *roasts* came out dry, unfortunately.

gloss: A boneless piece of meat or fish.
examples: Two salmon *fillets*, please, and hold the sauce.
The chicken *fillet* was overcooked.
Each *fillet* takes about six minutes per side.
contrast: Americans say fih-LAY; the British say FIL-it. Same word, and the US often spells it "filet".

gloss: The lower leg of a chicken or turkey, eaten as food.
examples: The kids always fight over the *drumsticks*.
He grabbed a *drumstick* off the platter.
*Drumsticks* are the cheapest part of the bird.

gloss: The arm of a bird, eaten as food, usually fried or grilled with sauce.
examples: We ordered twenty *wings* for the game.
This *wing* is barely cooked.
Their buffalo *wings* are the best in town.

gloss: The upper leg of a chicken or turkey, eaten as food.
examples: Chicken *thighs* stay juicier than breasts.
She browned six *thighs* in the pan.
One *thigh* is plenty for me.
contrast: The gh is silent — THY, one syllable, rhyming with "my".

gloss: The front meat of a bird, the leanest part.
examples: Two chicken *breasts* will feed all of us.
Slice the *breast* thin for the sandwiches.
Turkey *breast* dries out if you leave it too long.
contrast: The ea is short — BREST, rhyming with "rest", not with "beast".

gloss: The large internal organ of an animal, eaten as food.
examples: *Liver* and onions was a weeknight staple growing up.
She sautéed the chicken *livers* with butter and sage.
I couldn't stand *liver* as a kid.

gloss: One of a pair of internal organs, eaten as food.
examples: Steak and *kidney* pie is a British thing, not an American one.
The *kidneys* need to soak before you cook them.
He'll eat almost any organ meat except *kidney*.

gloss: The stomach lining of a cow or sheep, eaten as food.
examples: The soup had *tripe* in it, which I wasn't expecting.
*Tripe* has to be cleaned and boiled for a long time.
You'll find *tripe* in menudo and in plenty of other stews.

gloss: The soft fatty tissue inside bones, eaten as a delicacy.
examples: They served roasted bones so you could scoop out the *marrow*.
*Marrow* makes the broth rich.
He spread the *marrow* on toast with a little salt.

gloss: A muscular part of a bird's stomach, eaten as food.
examples: Fried *gizzards* are a Southern snack.
She simmered the *gizzard* with the neck to make stock.
The bag inside the turkey holds the liver and the *gizzard*.

gloss: The tail of a cow, cut into pieces and cooked slowly.
examples: *Oxtail* stew takes all afternoon and it's worth it.
She browned the *oxtails* before adding the stock.
*Oxtail* used to be cheap and now it isn't.

gloss: The heart, liver, and gizzard of a bird, packed separately inside it.
examples: Don't forget to pull the *giblets* out before roasting the turkey.
She uses the *giblets* to make gravy.
The *giblets* come in a little paper bag.
contrast: The g is soft — JIB-lits, not "GIB-lits". Almost always used in the plural.

gloss: The internal organs of an animal used as food.
examples: Nose-to-tail restaurants put a lot of *offal* on the menu.
*Offal* is cheap, nutritious, and unpopular.
He grew up eating *offal* and doesn't think twice about it.
contrast: Sounds just like "awful" — AW-fuhl. Context is the only thing that separates them.

gloss: A hard, spiced, dry-cured sausage eaten in thin slices.
examples: Put a little *salami* on the cheese board.
They hang the *salamis* in the back of the shop.
He built a sandwich out of *salami*, provolone, and hot peppers.

gloss: A spicy dry sausage, sliced thin and used mainly on pizza.
examples: Half *pepperoni*, half mushroom.
The *pepperoni* curled up into little cups in the oven.
He picks the *pepperoni* off and eats it first.

gloss: Italian dry-cured ham served in very thin slices.
examples: Wrap the melon in *prosciutto*.
Good *prosciutto* is worth the money.
She laid the *prosciutto* over the top of the pizza after it came out.
contrast: The sci is one sh sound — pruh-SHOO-toh, never "pros-kee-OO-toh".

gloss: Beef that has been brined, coated in spices, smoked, and steamed.
examples: *Pastrami* on rye with a pickle.
That deli piles the *pastrami* four inches high.
The *pastrami* was still warm when they sliced it.

gloss: A soft, mild, finely ground sausage sold in round slices for sandwiches.
examples: I ate a *bologna* sandwich every day in third grade.
Fried *bologna* is better than it sounds.
There's a pack of *bologna* in the meat drawer.
contrast: Written -gna but said "-ny": buh-LOH-nee, rhyming with "pony". Often respelled "baloney".

gloss: Meat cut into strips, seasoned, and dried so it keeps for a long time.
examples: I threw some *jerky* in my backpack for the hike.
Beef *jerky* costs a fortune at gas stations.
He makes his own *jerky* in a dehydrator.

gloss: A spicy pork sausage seasoned heavily with paprika or chili.
examples: Crumble the *chorizo* into the pan with the eggs.
There's *chorizo* in the tacos, so they're pretty spicy.
The *chorizo* left a layer of red oil in the skillet.

gloss: A fresh German-style pork sausage, usually grilled.
examples: He grilled *bratwursts* and served them with mustard.
One *bratwurst* split open on the grill.
The stand sells *bratwurst* and beer, and that's it.
contrast: In English the w is a normal w — BRAHT-wurst, not the German "v" sound.

gloss: A large farm bird eaten especially at Thanksgiving, or its meat.
examples: The *turkey* has to go in the oven by ten.
I'll take a *turkey* club, no mayo.
Two *turkeys* wandered across the road in front of us.
contrast: The bird is lowercase *turkey*; capital-T Turkey is the country.

gloss: A water bird eaten as food, or its rich dark meat.
examples: The roast *duck* was the best thing on the table.
*Duck* has a lot more fat than chicken.
They ordered two *ducks* for the party.

gloss: A small long-eared animal, or its lean pale meat.
examples: *Rabbit* tastes a lot like chicken, honestly.
The stew was made with two *rabbits* and a lot of wine.
You can't buy *rabbit* at most American supermarkets.

gloss: Fish and shellfish eaten as food.
examples: There's great *seafood* all along the coast.
She's allergic to *seafood*, so skip the shrimp.
The *seafood* here comes in fresh every morning.

gloss: A sea creature with a shell, such as a crab, clam, or lobster, eaten as food.
examples: He has a *shellfish* allergy, so no crab cakes.
The *shellfish* were harvested that morning.
Steam the *shellfish* just until they open.
contrast: The plural is *shellfish*, unchanged — never "shellfishes".

gloss: A large sea creature with claws, eaten as food.
examples: We split a *lobster* and a bottle of white wine.
The *lobsters* were still in the tank.
*Lobster* used to be considered poor people's food.

gloss: A sea creature with a flat shell and claws, eaten as food.
examples: We caught a dozen *crabs* off the pier.
The *crab* cakes here are mostly filler.
Fresh *crab* is worth the mess.

gloss: A shellfish with a rough shell, usually eaten raw.
examples: A dozen *oysters* on the half shell, please.
He swallowed the *oyster* whole and made a face.
The *oysters* were briny and ice cold.

gloss: A shellfish with two hinged shells, eaten steamed, fried, or in soup.
examples: We dug *clams* on the beach at low tide.
Throw out any *clam* that won't open.
The chowder had almost no *clams* in it.

gloss: A small shellfish with a dark blue-black shell, usually steamed.
examples: Steam the *mussels* in white wine and garlic.
Every *mussel* opened except two.
They serve *mussels* with fries, Belgian style.
contrast: Sounds exactly like "muscle" (мышца) — MUH-suhl, and the c in "muscle" is silent.

gloss: A shellfish with a fan-shaped shell, of which the round white muscle is eaten.
examples: Sear the *scallops* about ninety seconds a side.
One *scallop* was still cold in the middle.
*Scallops* go rubbery the second you overcook them.
contrast: Two pronunciations are both standard in the US: SKAH-luhp and SKAL-uhp.

gloss: A shellfish like a large shrimp, eaten as food.
examples: The curry came with four enormous *prawns*.
He peeled the *prawn* and ate it in one bite.
Grilled *prawns* were the best thing we ate all trip.
contrast: Americans say "shrimp" for almost everything; *prawn* is much more common in British and Australian English.

gloss: A small freshwater shellfish that looks like a tiny lobster.
examples: They boiled forty pounds of *crawfish* for the party.
You suck the head and eat the tail of the *crawfish*.
*Crawfish* season runs through the spring down there.
contrast: Also spelled "crayfish"; the plural stays *crawfish*, with no -es.

gloss: A very small, strongly salted fish, usually sold packed in oil.
examples: Two *anchovies* melted into the sauce add a lot of depth.
She ordered the Caesar without *anchovy*.
There's a tin of *anchovies* in the back of the cabinet.
contrast: Stress can fall either way in the US: AN-choh-vee and an-CHOH-vee are both heard.

gloss: A small oily fish, usually sold canned.
examples: He eats *sardines* on toast for lunch.
The can held six *sardines* in olive oil.
One *sardine* has more calcium than you'd think.
contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable: sar-DEEN, not "SAR-deen".

gloss: A very large flatfish with firm white meat.
examples: The *halibut* was grilled with lemon and butter.
They pulled in two *halibut* that morning.
*Halibut* is expensive but almost impossible to ruin.
contrast: The plural is usually *halibut*, unchanged.

gloss: A mild white farmed fish, sold cheaply as fillets.
examples: *Tilapia* is the cheapest fish at our store.
She baked the *tilapia* with breadcrumbs on top.
Two *tilapia* fillets feed the whole family.

gloss: A freshwater fish with long feelers around its mouth, often fried.
examples: Fried *catfish* and hush puppies is a Friday tradition.
He caught three *catfish* off the dock.
*Catfish* has a muddier flavor than tilapia.
contrast: The plural is *catfish*, unchanged.

gloss: A flat fish that lies on the sea floor, with delicate white meat.
examples: The *flounder* was so thin it cooked in four minutes.
They were catching *flounder* right off the beach.
*Flounder* falls apart if you flip it too much.
contrast: The plural is *flounder*, unchanged. Don't confuse it with the verb "to flounder" (барахтаться).

gloss: A small flatfish with fine white meat.
examples: She ordered the *sole* with brown butter.
*Sole* is mild enough that kids will eat it.
Two pieces of *sole* were plenty for dinner.
contrast: Sounds exactly like "soul" (душа), and is spelled like the sole of a shoe.

gloss: A warm-water fish with firm meat, often served whole.
examples: The red *snapper* came out whole with the head on.
They were selling *snapper* right off the boat.
*Snapper* holds up well on the grill.

gloss: A large warm-water fish with thick white meat.
examples: A blackened *grouper* sandwich is the move down there.
*Grouper* is meaty enough to hold together in a stew.
He hooked a *grouper* big enough to fill the cooler.

gloss: A long snake-like fish, often served grilled or smoked.
examples: Grilled *eel* over rice is worth trying at least once.
The tank at the market was full of live *eels*.
Smoked *eel* is much fattier than I expected.

gloss: Salted fish eggs, especially from sturgeon, eaten as a delicacy.
examples: They served *caviar* on tiny blini.
A spoonful of *caviar* costs more than the whole meal.
Real *caviar* should taste of the sea, not of salt.

gloss: The mass of eggs inside a female fish, eaten as food.
examples: The sushi was topped with orange *roe*.
Salmon *roe* pops when you bite it.
They sell the *roe* separately from the fish.
contrast: Sounds exactly like "row" (ряд) — ROH.

gloss: Squid served as food, usually cut into rings and fried.
examples: We started with fried *calamari*.
The *calamari* was chewy and under-seasoned.
Their *calamari* comes with marinara on the side.

gloss: Salt-cured salmon, sliced thin and usually eaten on a bagel.
examples: A bagel with cream cheese and *lox*, please.
The *lox* was sliced so thin you could see through it.
He'd never had *lox* until he moved to New York.
contrast: Sounds exactly like "locks" (замки) — LAHKS.

gloss: A small rectangular piece of breaded fish, sold frozen.
examples: Dinner was *fish sticks* and ketchup again.
He ate every *fish stick* on the plate but no vegetables.
There's a bag of *fish sticks* in the freezer.
contrast: Called "fish fingers" in British English.

gloss: Milk and the foods made from it, taken together.
examples: He cut out *dairy* and felt better within a week.
The *dairy* aisle is on the far wall.
This recipe has no *dairy* in it at all.
contrast: DEH-ree — not to be confused with "diary" (дневник), which is DYE-uh-ree.

gloss: A solid food made from milk that has been curdled and pressed.
examples: Grate a little *cheese* over the top.
They carry about forty different *cheeses*.
I could live on bread and *cheese*.

gloss: A soft yellow fat made by churning cream.
examples: Let the *butter* soften before you start.
There's a stick of *butter* in the door of the fridge.
She uses way too much *butter*, and that's why it tastes good.

gloss: The thick fatty part that rises to the top of milk.
examples: Do you take *cream* in your coffee?
Stir a little *cream* into the sauce at the end.
The *cream* had gone sour, so I threw it out.

gloss: A thick, slightly sour food made by fermenting milk.
examples: She has *yogurt* and berries every morning.
Grab a couple of *yogurts* while you're there.
Plain *yogurt* works fine in place of sour cream.
contrast: US YOH-gurt with a long o; the British say YOG-urt and spell it "yoghurt".

gloss: The tangy liquid left after churning butter, or a cultured drink like it.
examples: Soak the chicken in *buttermilk* overnight.
*Buttermilk* is what makes these pancakes fluffy.
If you don't have *buttermilk*, add lemon juice to milk.

gloss: The soft solid part that separates from milk when it sours or is treated.
examples: Cheese *curds* squeak when they're fresh.
The *curd* is cut and drained before pressing.
Poutine is fries, gravy, and cheese *curds*.

gloss: The watery liquid left when milk separates into curds.
examples: Drain off the *whey* and keep the solids.
*Whey* protein is in almost every shake on the shelf.
There was a thin layer of *whey* on top of the yogurt.
contrast: Sounds exactly like "way" (путь) — WAY.

gloss: A soft white Italian cheese that melts and stretches when heated.
examples: Fresh *mozzarella* with tomatoes and basil, that's the whole dish.
The *mozzarella* browned in spots under the broiler.
Buy the *mozzarella* packed in water, not the shredded kind.
contrast: The zz is a ts sound — mah-tsuh-REH-luh, not "moz-uh-REL-uh".

gloss: A soft, mild, grainy white cheese made from whey.
examples: Spread the *ricotta* between the layers of lasagna.
*Ricotta* on toast with honey is a great breakfast.
The filling is *ricotta*, egg, and a lot of parsley.

gloss: A salty white cheese, traditionally Greek, that crumbles easily.
examples: Crumble some *feta* over the salad.
The *feta* comes in brine, so drain it first.
*Feta* is salty enough that you can skip the salt.

gloss: Soft tangy cheese made from goat's milk.
examples: The beet salad had *goat cheese* on it.
*Goat cheese* is easier on my stomach than regular cheese.
Spread the *goat cheese* on while the toast is still warm.

gloss: Strong-smelling cheese streaked with blue-green mold.
examples: Wings come with ranch or *blue cheese*.
The *blue cheese* was so strong it took over the salad.
He put *blue cheese* on the burger, which I'd never tried before.

gloss: A soft white cheese of loose curds, eaten fresh.
examples: She eats *cottage cheese* with pineapple.
There's a tub of *cottage cheese* behind the milk.
*Cottage cheese* is having a comeback for some reason.

gloss: A soft, mild, spreadable cheese made from cream and milk.
examples: Just a little *cream cheese* on the bagel, not a mountain of it.
Let the *cream cheese* come to room temperature first.
The frosting is butter, sugar, and *cream cheese*.

gloss: Cream that has been soured with bacteria to make it thick and tangy.
examples: Put a spoonful of *sour cream* on the chili.
We're out of *sour cream* — use yogurt.
The baked potato came loaded with *sour cream* and chives.

gloss: Cream beaten until it holds soft peaks, usually sweetened.
examples: Do you want *whipped cream* on that?
She made the *whipped cream* by hand, which took forever.
The pie was covered in *whipped cream*.

gloss: A mix of equal parts milk and cream, used mainly in coffee.
examples: There's *half-and-half* in the fridge if you want it.
He takes his coffee black, no *half-and-half*.
The diner puts little cups of *half-and-half* on every table.
contrast: An American product; British and Australian speakers usually just say "single cream" or "milk".

ru: сливки для кофе (в т. ч. сухие)
gloss: A liquid or powder added to coffee in place of cream.
examples: The office only has powdered *creamer*.
She uses vanilla *creamer* in everything.
We're out of *creamer* again.

gloss: A sweet frozen dessert made from cream, sugar, and flavoring.
examples: Let's get *ice cream* after dinner.
The *ice cream* melted before we got to the car.
They have about thirty different *ice creams* behind the counter.

gloss: Italian-style frozen dessert, denser and less fatty than ice cream.
examples: The *gelato* place on the corner stays open until midnight.
*Gelato* is softer than ice cream because it's served warmer.
She got pistachio *gelato* and finished it in about a minute.
contrast: The g is soft — juh-LAH-toh, not "guh-LAH-toh".

gloss: A thick sweet mixture of milk or cream cooked with eggs.
examples: The tart was filled with a vanilla *custard*.
Stir the *custard* constantly or it will scramble.
Frozen *custard* is richer than soft serve.

gloss: A soft, creamy sweet dessert made with milk.
examples: There's chocolate *pudding* for dessert.
She packed a *pudding* cup in his lunch.
The *puddings* set in the fridge overnight.
contrast: The u is short, as in "put". In the US a *pudding* is one specific creamy dessert; in Britain it can mean dessert in general.

gloss: A tangy fermented milk drink, thinner than yogurt.
examples: He drinks a glass of *kefir* every morning.
*Kefir* is thinner than yogurt and a lot more sour.
They sell plain and strawberry *kefir* at the co-op.
contrast: In American English the stress falls on the second syllable: kuh-FEER.

gloss: A butter substitute made from vegetable oil.
examples: My grandmother baked with *margarine* her whole life.
This says butter, but you can use *margarine*.
*Margarine* doesn't brown the way butter does.
contrast: The g is soft — MAR-juh-rin, even though the spelling says "gar".

gloss: Soft white fat rendered from a pig, used for cooking and baking.
examples: Real tamales are made with *lard*.
*Lard* makes the flakiest pie crust there is.
She keeps a tub of *lard* by the stove.

gloss: The natural sugar found in milk.
examples: He can't digest *lactose*, so he drinks oat milk.
Aged cheeses have very little *lactose* left in them.
The label says the *lactose* has been removed.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: The greasy substance in meat and dairy products.
examples: Trim the *fat* off before you grill it.
Whole milk has more *fat* than skim.
Not all *fats* are bad for you.

gloss: The oval object laid by a hen, eaten as food.
examples: How do you want your *eggs*?
Crack the *egg* into a separate bowl first.
We're down to two *eggs*, so no pancakes.

gloss: The round yellow center of an egg.
examples: The *yolk* was still runny, exactly right.
Separate the *yolks* from the whites.
He broke the *yolk* trying to flip it.
contrast: The l is silent — YOHK, sounding exactly like "yoke" (ярмо).

gloss: The clear part of an egg that turns white when cooked.
examples: He orders an *egg white* omelet every time.
Beat the *egg whites* until they hold peaks.
One *egg white* has almost no fat in it.

gloss: The thin hard outer covering of an egg.
examples: There's a piece of *eggshell* in the batter.
She puts crushed *eggshells* in the garden.
The *eggshell* cracked but the egg didn't break.

gloss: Beaten eggs cooked flat in a pan and usually folded over a filling.
examples: I'll have a cheese *omelet* and coffee.
He folded the *omelet* too soon and it tore.
They make *omelets* to order at the hotel.
contrast: The usual American spelling is *omelet*; the British write "omelette".

gloss: Egg whites beaten with sugar and baked until crisp or lightly browned.
examples: The lemon pie had two inches of *meringue* on top.
She piped the *meringues* onto parchment paper.
*Meringue* weeps if you make it on a humid day.
contrast: The -gue is silent: muh-RANG, rhyming with "rang".

gloss: An open pastry shell filled with a baked mixture of eggs and cream.
examples: She brought a *quiche* to the brunch.
The *quiche* is better at room temperature.
They had two *quiches* left at the end of the day.
contrast: One syllable, KEESH, despite the French spelling.

gloss: The thin liquid left from cooking meat, fish, or vegetables in water.
examples: Simmer the noodles in chicken *broth*, not water.
She drank the *broth* and left the vegetables.
There's a carton of beef *broth* in the pantry.

gloss: A sauce made from meat juices thickened with flour.
examples: Pour the *gravy* over the mashed potatoes.
His *gravy* came out lumpy.
There's never enough *gravy* at Thanksgiving.

gloss: The hard outer layer of a cheese, or the skin of a piece of pork.
examples: Save the Parmesan *rind* and throw it in the soup.
Some *rinds* are edible and some aren't.
Pork *rind* is basically fried pig skin.
